title: Fallback policy playbook & on-call intake with Arboreal Systems
summary: Discovery focused on incident tolerance, multi-region steering and an on-call fallback playbook. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for latency-sensitive inference endpoints; primary concerns: regional failover, KV cache consistency, auditability, and predictable cost under degraded modes.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — this is Maya from Redwood. we have Ravi, our solutions engineer, and Imani from customer success. how's everyone?
[00:07] Taylor (Arboreal): Hi, thanks. Taylor here, glad to be on. we have Sam – our SRE – and Lena from security.
[00:12] Sam (SRE): hey, yeah, thanks. curious to hear the runway for failure modes.
[00:18] Ravi (SE): Great. I'll try to keep the deep stuff in the middle, but happy to go into kernel selection and kv cache behavior if you want.
[00:26] Lena (Security): quick ask: we'll need proof points for audit logging and KMS integration. SOC 2 is a must.
[00:33] Maya: noted. we have SOC 2 + ISO docs, and KMS/HSM integration is available for Private and Dedicated. we'll share the security pack after.
[00:41] Taylor: high level context: Arboreal runs inference for real-time underwriting — 95th pctl latency matters; if a region degrades we need graceful fallback without massive cost spikes.
[00:53] Ravi: ok, two orthogonal things: routing and model variant fallback; and retention / cache concerns. do you have a preferred regional failover strategy? active-active or active-passive?
[01:03] Sam: right now active-active in front of a load balancer but our model is sensitive to token latency — we sometimes accept small latency increases for cost savings.
[01:12] Maya: for hosted we offer region steering policies — you can set latency vs cost priority; if latency exceeds X ms we route to a hot fallback model or different region.
[01:22] Taylor: how deterministic is that? i.e. consistent steering during partial network partitions?
[01:29] Ravi: the control plane monitors egress and health signals; in network partitions we fall back to routing by last-known healthy region, and we have a circuit breaker with gradual failover to prevent a thundering herd. sometimes the transcriber says "thunder" — but we actually use a token bucket + leaky bucket style circuit.
[01:45] Sam: what about KV cache? our prefix cache is critical to keep latency low.
[01:50] Ravi: two options: shared KV cache in Dedicated/Private where cache can be replicated cross-zone, or per-region caches with eventual consistency. for strict consistency we recommend Dedicated with synchronous replication, but that's higher cost. per-region caches reduce tail latency but you get cache misses on region switches.
[02:07] Lena: and how do you ensure PII doesn't leak in cache?
[02:11] Imani (CSM): we have configurable cache retention policies, redaction hooks, and the option to disable prefix caching per-route for sensitive prompts.
[02:20] Taylor: can we configure time-to-live by route? e.g., underwriting route 1 min, analytics routes 1 hour?
[02:26] Maya: yes, TTL per route. and Redwood Optimize will recommend cache parameters based on observed hit rates.
[02:33] Sam: service-level objectives — you publish SLOs for hosted vs dedicated?
[02:37] Maya: hosted: best-effort low-latency with region options, we publish 99th pctl baselines; Dedicated: we offer reserved capacity with SLA-backed availability and percentile latency targets depending on the commit.
[02:50] Sam: what's the failover RTO you'd expect if a region is fully down?
[02:54] Ravi: typical warm-fallback is under 30s for hot-standby regions with session-less requests. if you need KV warmstart and sticky context it can be longer, 2–5 minutes depending on cache priming and warmup.
[03:06] Taylor: 2–5 minutes is a big range — what can we do to reduce that?
[03:10] Ravi: pre-warming via traffic shadowing and priming popular prefixes into the fallback model; also using a lightweight 1.5B variant on fallback to keep latency shallow while heavier models spin up.
[03:21] Sam: that implies model variants — how seamless is the output quality when we switch to a smaller quantized model?
[03:27] Maya: Redwood Optimize helps pick quantization levels and suggests fallback variants with rollbacks. customers often accept slight quality degradation for availability. we can add A/B monitoring to detect regressions.
[03:38] Lena: legal will want an SLA table showing availability guarantees and credits. do you include credits for partial degradation?
[03:44] Maya: yes, for Dedicated we include uptime credits; for hosted we have a published uptime target but different credit structure. for partial degradation clauses we can discuss specific thresholds — e.g., error rate > X or 95th pctl latency > Y triggers a partial SLA credit.
[03:59] Taylor: latency vs cost tradeoff — does Redwood automatically shift to a lower-cost region during outbreaks?
[04:05] Ravi: policy-driven. you can set strict latency-first or cost-first. strict latency will never send to lower-cost region unless a circuit opens; cost-first can redirect to cheaper variants.
[04:15] Sam: curious about observability ties — how do we trace a request from our edge LB through Redwood to the model and back?
[04:21] Imani: we provide request-level traces and token-level latency breakdowns. there are also hooks for your tracing system — we export spans to OTLP exporters and include trace IDs in logs.
[04:31] Taylor: good. send us an example trace output.
[04:34] Maya: will do.
[04:36] [05:00] (short side discussion about billing metering)
[05:12] Ravi: note that during failover we meter tokens differently for fallback variants — we'll surface the expected unit cost for the fallback mix in the pricing model.
[05:24] Taylor: important for us — we don't want a surprise 4x cost during incidents.
[05:29] Maya: understood. we'll model the worst-case costs in the pilot.
[05:34] Sam: any customer references who did multi-region failovers?
[05:38] Maya: yes, we have a couple — i can share a short case study with regional failover playbook.
[05:44] Lena: security again — audit logs need to show who flipped any routing policy and when.
[05:49] Ravi: audit logs include policy changes, API keys, rollout events, and can be exported to your SIEM. we also retain an immutable event stream for Private deployments if required.
[05:59] Taylor: we will likely start with a pilot on Dedicated in one region, then expand to multi-region Dedicated or Private depending on cost. timeline target is end of Q1 for a pilot.
[06:10] Maya: perfect. let's talk on-call playbooks — how does Redwood recommend runbooks be structured?
[06:16] Ravi: short version: detect, isolate, fallback, remediate, ramp back. include clear thresholds (latency/err rate), who to page, and an automated routing toggle with a safe rollback window.
[06:29] Sam: who owns the toggle? platform or Redwood?
[06:33] Maya: it's configurable — you can give platform teams the toggle or Redwood can manage in an operational runbook under a managed-services agreement.
[06:41] Taylor: can we test failover with a scheduled game-day?
[06:45] Ravi: yes, Redwood supports chaos testing — we can run simulated region outages in a sandbox and report cache miss surge impacts and recovery timelines.
[06:55] [07:10] (audio artifact: short cough, small cross talk)
[07:20] Sam: about caching again — if we go private on prem, we want to use our own KMS. is that supported?
[07:27] Ravi: yes, Private supports customer-managed KMS and you can opt into HSM-backed keys. Dedicated can also integrate with your cloud KMS for key wrapping.
[07:36] Lena: what about logs residency and retention? we need 7 years for some artifacts.
[07:40] Maya: retention is configurable per deployment; for Private we support long retention with direct object-store integration. for hosted we have retention tiers and log export options.
[07:50] Taylor: cool. any gotchas with session affinity during region failovers?
[07:55] Ravi: session affinity is sticky via a session token; if region fails you'll either rehydrate or fall back to stateless operation. rehydration cost/time again depends on cache priming strategies.
[08:08] Sam: the team is also worried about double billing during retry storms — is there dedup support?
[08:13] Maya: we have idempotency keys and edge-side dedup heuristics; in severe retries we throttle and surface retry stats so you can tune client-side backoff.
[08:23] Taylor: great. i'd like a short runbook template we can adapt.
[08:27] Imani: we'll attach a template.
[08:30] [09:00] (longer section where Ravi shares architecture diagram link: https://redwood.ai/arch/failover-sample — said quickly, may be transcribed wrong)
[09:10] Ravi: one more thing — quantization fallback paths can cause a style change in outputs; we recommend feature flags to label fallback responses to help downstream ranking systems.
[09:22] Sam: can we get per-request labels?
[09:25] Ravi: yes, metadata tags on responses and trace IDs.
[09:29] Taylor: what's the typical pilot scope you recommend?
[09:33] Maya: pilot: lift-and-shift 1–2 endpoints to Dedicated with steady-state traffic mirrored from your prod for 2–4 weeks; run a chaos test, validate metrics, and iterate.
[09:43] Taylor: budget wise — rough estimate?
[09:46] Maya: i'll share a cost model but expect dedicated reserved capacity with baseline commit; we'll show a worst-case incident cost delta.
[09:55] [10:00] (customer asks about compliance questionnaire turnaround)
[10:04] Imani: typical turnaround 48–72 hours for security pack; longer if bespoke contracts.
[10:10] Lena: we'll send our questionnaire by EOD.
[10:13] Maya: great.
[10:15] [10:45] (discussion moves to decision stakeholders and timelines)
[10:52] Taylor: decision owner is Taylor, procurement hit mid-Feb, target pilot sign by 2026-03-01.
[10:59] Maya: noted.
[11:03] Sam: one final technical — do you support traffic split weighting during degrade? e.g., 80/20 to primary vs fallback?
[11:10] Ravi: yes, traffic-split policies are configurable and can be automatic based on health or manual.
[11:16] Taylor: ok, that helps.
[11:18] Maya: let's recap next steps and action items.
[11:22] [11:30] (recap)
[11:32] Maya: Action items: we'll send security pack, pricing model with incident cost scenarios, runbook template, a sample trace, and a case study. Taylor will send questionnaire and share final pilot stakeholders.
[11:45] Taylor: thanks all.
[11:48] Maya: talk soon.
[11:50] (meeting ends)

Imani Cole (CSM): Provide security pack and SOC2/ISO artifacts — due 2026-01-20
Ravi Patel (SE): Share architecture diagram, example trace output, and runbook template — due 2026-01-20
Taylor Reed (Arboreal): Send security questionnaire and finalized pilot stakeholder list — due 2026-01-19
next_steps: Redwood to deliver security pack + sample traces + pricing by 2026-01-22
Schedule a technical pilot kickoff (Dedicated, single region) week of 2026-02-02
Run chaos failover test during pilot and review results week 2 of pilot
